presentations.name: Working memory difficulty
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty HOLDING and WORKING ON information in mind for a few seconds while doing something else with it — keeping a sentence in mind while writing it, carrying a number in mental arithmetic, remembering step three while doing step one.

•  Baddeley and Hitch (1974) framed working memory as a limited-capacity system (phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive); Baddeley (2000) added the episodic buffer. The classroom question is which of these is overloaded, not whether the child 'has' it.

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis. Part D lists it as 'Executive function profile, not a diagnosis' — nobody diagnoses it, and it needs no diagnosis t

presentations.name: Inhibition difficulty
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty STOPPING or HOLDING BACK a response — the answer shouted out, the hand that reaches before the thought, the comment said before it is checked. Diamond (2013) groups inhibitory control (self-control and interference control) as one of three core executive functions.

•  Barkley (1997) places behavioural inhibition at the centre of his account of self-regulation: without the pause, the other executive functions do not get a chance to operate.

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis (Part D). It is described, formulated and supported; nobody diagnoses it.

•  It shows in two forms: MOTOR/BEHAVIOURAL (blurting, touching, grabbing, leaving the seat) and COG

presentations.name: Cognitive flexibility difficulty
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty SHIFTING — between tasks, rules, perspectives or strategies. Diamond (2013) names cognitive flexibility as the third core executive function, building on inhibition and working memory.

•  In class it looks like: stuck on one method when it isn't working, distress when the timetable changes, difficulty seeing another person's view in a dispute, repeating an error after being shown the fix.

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it; you describe the situations where shifting breaks down.

•  Zelazo's Dimensional Change Card Sort (Zelazo, 2006) shows the developmental shape: younger children know the new rule and still sort by

presentations.name: Planning and organisation difficulty
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty working out the STEPS to a goal, putting them in ORDER and managing TIME — planning an essay, sequencing a science practical, breaking a project into weeks.

•  Dawson and Guare (2018) treat planning/prioritisation, organisation and time management as distinct executive skills; separating them tells you which support to write.

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis (Part D). Distinct from 'Organisation of materials' (physical belongings), which is its own presentation.

•  Load rises sharply when tasks become longer, less structured and more self-directed — typically late primary and the move to post-primary.

presentations.name: Task initiation difficulty
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty GETTING STARTED on a task at the point it is set, even when the child has the skill to do it. Dawson and Guare (2018) list task initiation as a distinct executive skill.

•  Classroom signature: sharpening pencils, looking around, asking to go to the toilet, sitting with a blank page after everyone else has begun.

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

•  Several different mechanisms produce the same blank page: not knowing where to start (planning), not having held the instruction (working memory), fear of getting it wrong (anxiety), low energy (mood or sleep), or finding the task unreadable (literacy).

2 · WHAT IT IS

presentations.name: Self-monitoring difficulty
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty CHECKING one's own work, behaviour and effect on others while it is happening or afterwards — not noticing errors, not noticing that a peer is annoyed, handing in work unchecked.

•  Draws on metacognition — thinking about one's own thinking (Flavell, 1979). BRIEF-2 separates Self-Monitor (awareness of own behaviour and its effect) from Task-Monitor (checking work).

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

•  Often explains the 'careless error' pattern: the child can find and fix the error when asked, but did not look.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT carelessness as an attitude. The child usually cares about the result and is

presentations.name: Motivation and engagement with work
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of how much the pupil INVESTS in school tasks — behaviourally (does the work), emotionally (cares about it) and cognitively (thinks hard about it). Fredricks, Blumenfeld and Paris (2004) set out these three dimensions of engagement.

•  Motivation is not a fixed trait: Self-Determination Theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000) links it to autonomy, competence and relatedness; expectancy-value theory (Eccles & Wigfield, 2002) to 'can I do it?' and 'is it worth it?'.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D lists it as 'Added — not in the conditions index'). Nobody diagnoses low motivation.

•  It is almost always the END of a chain — repeated failure, an unidenti

presentations.name: Work rate and pace of output
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  The pupil produces LESS work, or takes MUCH LONGER, than peers of similar ability — unfinished copies, unfinished tests, homework taking hours.

•  Slow output is a final common pathway: processing speed, handwriting speed, spelling retrieval, reading speed, attention, perfectionism and fatigue all produce it. The assessment task is to find which.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses slow work rate.

•  Processing speed develops through childhood and adolescence (Kail, 1991); a WISC-V Processing Speed Index describes speed on simple visual tasks, which is not the same as classroom output speed.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT the same as low abi

presentations.name: Homework completion and follow-through
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Homework not recorded, not brought home, not started, not finished or not handed in — each a DIFFERENT failure point in a chain that runs from the classroom to the kitchen table and back.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

•  Cooper, Robinson and Patall (2006) found the homework–achievement association stronger at secondary than at primary; at primary, the bigger risk is homework becoming a nightly conflict that damages the parent–child relationship.

•  Langberg et al. (2012) developed the HOPS programme for middle-school pupils with ADHD, targeting homework recording, materials and planning — the chain, not the attitude.

presentations.name: Organisation of materials, books and equipment
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty KEEPING TRACK of physical belongings: wrong books, lost copies, no pencil, overflowing bag and locker, crumpled notes, PE gear forgotten.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). BRIEF-2 has a separate Organisation of Materials scale on the parent and teacher forms; check the manual.

•  Distinct from planning (organising steps and time). A pupil can plan an essay well and still arrive without the copy it's in.

•  Abikoff et al. (2013) targeted materials management alongside time and planning in Organizational Skills Training and found improvements in ADHD samples.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT carelessness about school. Most pupils are embarrassed by

presentations.name: Sustained attention in whole-class vs one-to-one
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A pupil who ATTENDS WELL one-to-one (with you, with the SET) but drifts, fidgets or disengages in whole-class teaching. The gap itself is the finding.

•  One-to-one gives constant adult proximity, immediate feedback, controlled pace, one voice and low noise; whole-class removes all of these at once. The question is which one matters for this pupil.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

•  It is a well-recognised limitation of assessment: the testing room is close to ideal conditions, so test attention can overestimate classroom attention (Barkley, 2015, discusses this for clinic assessment).

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT evidence that the

presentations.name: Note-taking and recording from the board
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty getting information from the board, screen or teacher's speech into a copy accurately and in time. It stacks several demands: look up, find place, hold a chunk in working memory, look down, spell, write, look up again.

•  Far-point copying (board) is harder than near-point copying (from a sheet on the desk) because of the repeated shift in gaze and place-finding.

•  Note-taking from speech adds listening, selecting and summarising in real time. Kiewra (1985) found the benefit of notes comes from both encoding and later review.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT simply laziness or messiness — the

presentations.name: Study skills and revision strategy
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  The pupil works hard but studies INEFFICIENTLY — re-reading, highlighting and copying notes — and results do not reflect the time spent.

•  Dunlosky et al. (2013) reviewed ten learning techniques: practice testing and distributed practice were rated HIGH utility; highlighting, re-reading and summarisation LOW. Most pupils use the low-utility ones.

•  Roediger and Karpicke (2006) showed retrieval practice (testing yourself) produced better long-term retention than restudying, even though restudying felt more effective.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a character issue. Study strategy is rarely taught exp

presentations.name: Help-seeking
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Whether the pupil knows WHEN they need help, WHO to ask and HOW to ask — and does so. Part D lists it under 1.1 as 'knowing when and how to ask'; help-seeking from adults in relationships sits separately under 4.2.

•  Nelson-Le Gall (1981) framed help-seeking as a problem-solving skill; Newman (2002) distinguishes ADAPTIVE help-seeking (asking for hints to solve it yourself) from EXECUTIVE help-seeking (asking for the answer).

•  Ryan, Pintrich and Midgley (2001) found pupils who most need help are often least likely to ask, with avoidance linked to perceived threat to competence.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

presentations.name: Fatigue, sleep and time-of-day effects on attention
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Attention, behaviour or work rate that VARIES by time of day, day of week or across a term in a way that tracks tiredness, sleep, hunger or (for some pupils) medication timing.

•  Astill et al. (2012) meta-analysed a century of research on sleep in school-age children and found shorter sleep associated with poorer cognitive performance and more behavioural problems.

•  Paruthi et al. (2016, American Academy of Sleep Medicine consensus) recommend 9–12 hours for children aged 6–12 and 8–10 hours for adolescents aged 13–18 per 24 hours.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it — sleep disorders themselves are a medical question.

presentations.name: AAC and communication access
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) is any method that supplements or replaces speech: unaided (sign, gesture — including Lámh, the Irish key word sign system) and aided (symbols, communication books, PODD, PECS, speech-generating devices).

•  Beukelman and Light (2020) define the aim as communicative competence across partners and settings, not use of a device for its own sake.

•  Part D: 'Not a DSM diagnosis.' It describes how a pupil accesses communication — and therefore access to assessment, learning and consent.

•  Communication ACCESS includes the partners: whether adults model the system, whether it is available all day, and whether vocabulary covers

presentations.name: English as an Additional Language (EAL)
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A pupil whose home or first language is not English, learning English (and often Irish) in school. Part D: 'Not a disorder — can mimic language disorder, rule out.'

•  Cummins distinguished conversational fluency (BICS) from academic language proficiency (CALP); the latter is widely cited as taking several years longer to develop (Cummins, 2008). Fluent playground English does not mean the pupil can access a textbook.

•  Newly arrived pupils may go through a non-verbal or 'silent' period (Tabors, 2008) — normal, not a sign of difficulty.

•  The key question for an EP is whether a difficulty exists IN BOTH (or all) languages — a true language disorder does; an EAL learnin

presentations.name: Bilingual language development
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Typical development of two (or more) languages — simultaneously from birth or sequentially. In Ireland this includes Irish-medium education (Gaelscoileanna, Gaeltacht schools) as well as home languages other than English.

•  Grosjean (1989): 'the bilingual is not two monolinguals in one person'. Vocabulary is distributed across languages; Pearson, Fernández and Oller (1993) found bilingual toddlers' total conceptual vocabulary comparable to monolinguals' when both languages were counted.

•  Hoff et al. (2012) found that language skill in each language tracks the amount of exposure to it — a lower score in one language often reflects less exposure, not difficulty.

•  Part

presentations.name: Vocabulary gap from limited exposure
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Vocabulary below age expectations because of LESS OPPORTUNITY — fewer conversations, fewer books, interrupted schooling, EAL — rather than a difficulty learning words.

•  Hart and Risley (1995) reported large differences in words heard by children in different socioeconomic groups; Sperry, Sperry and Miller (2019) challenged the size and generality of that 'word gap'. Romeo et al. (2018) found conversational turns, not just words heard, related to language and brain measures.

•  Stanovich (1986) described 'Matthew effects': children with more vocabulary read more and gain more vocabulary, widening gaps over time.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). The k

presentations.name: Participation in oral work and classroom talk
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  How much and how well the pupil contributes to spoken classroom activity — answering questions, discussion, group work, presentations. Part D notes this is Form 2 wording.

•  Oral participation is a learning tool, not just a behaviour: dialogic teaching approaches (Alexander, 2020; Mercer & Littleton, 2007) show talk is how pupils develop and test their thinking.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

•  Low participation is a common final pathway for language difficulty, anxiety, stammering, EAL, hearing loss, autism and cultural expectations about talking to adults.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT shyness by default. A pupil who does not t

presentations.name: Following multi-step verbal instructions
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of what the child does when an adult gives a spoken instruction with more than one step: they carry out the first or last part, stall, copy peers, or ask again. It is a behaviour seen in the classroom, not a diagnosis.

•  Following a spoken instruction draws on at least four things at once: HEARING it, UNDERSTANDING the words and grammar (especially 'before', 'after', 'unless', 'except'), HOLDING it in working memory, and ORGANISING the action. The presentation is the same whichever link breaks — the assessment is about finding which one.

•  Gathercole and colleagues showed in laboratory analogues of classroom tasks that children with low working memory lose

presentations.name: Narrative and sequencing in spoken account
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of how the child tells a story or recounts an event: whether there is a beginning, middle and end, whether events come in order, whether the listener can follow who did what, and whether causes and feelings are included.

•  Narrative is a demanding language task — it requires vocabulary, grammar, sequencing, perspective-taking and holding the whole story in mind. Story grammar models (Stein & Glenn, 1979) break it into setting, initiating event, internal response, attempt, consequence and reaction, which gives you a checklist for what is missing.

presentations.name: Word-finding difficulty
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A difficulty retrieving a word the child knows, at the moment it is needed. The child understands the word and may use it at other times, but in conversation or on demand it will not come.

•  It shows as long pauses, fillers ('um', 'the thing'), circumlocution ('the thing you cut with' for scissors), substituting a related word ('knife'), gesture, or giving up. Tip-of-the-tongue states are the everyday version.

•  Messer and Dockrell (2006) describe competing accounts: weak semantic representations (the word is only partly known) versus a retrieval or phonological access problem (the word is known but hard to reach). Which one applies shapes the intervention.

presentations.name: Interpreter need and how it changes the assessment
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Not a difficulty in the child — a condition of the assessment. Where the child, the parents, or both do not share a language with the EP well enough for informed consent, history-taking or feedback, a professional interpreter is needed, and the assessment itself changes.

•  It changes CONSENT (consent must be informed in a language the parent understands — PSI Code of Ethics; GDPR transparency), HISTORY (developmental history in the home language is often the best evidence of whether a difficulty exists in both languages), and TESTING (standardised verbal tests lose their norms when translated or interpreted).

•  Part D lists the NEPS interpreter request form as the route

presentations.name: Cognitive profile differences (verbal, fluid, working memory, processing speed)
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of unevenness across the indexes of a cognitive battery — typically WISC-V UK Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory and Processing Speed — where some areas are clearly stronger than others. It is a pattern in scores, not a condition.

•  Uneven profiles are common in the general population: a meaningful discrepancy between some pair of indexes is the norm rather than the exception. Check the base-rate tables in the WISC-V UK manual before calling any difference 'unusual'.

•  Its practical value is in explaining the child's experience of school — e.g. a child with strong verbal reasoning and slow processing speed who understands

presentations.name: Underachievement not meeting SLD criteria
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child whose attainment is lower than expected — from their age, their ability, their earlier progress, or their classmates — but whose difficulty does not meet criteria for a Specific Learning Disorder (DSM-5-TR) because it is not severe enough, not persistent despite targeted help, or better explained by something else.

•  The comparison matters and must be named: below AGE norms (low attainment), below what ABILITY predicts (underachievement in the classic sense), or below the child's OWN earlier trajectory (a falling-away). Each points to different causes.

•  IQ–achievement discrepancy on its own does not reliably distinguish children who need differ

presentations.name: Giftedness / exceptional ability
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child whose ability or performance in one or more areas is well above that of their peers. There is no single agreed definition: some models use high general ability, others domain-specific talent, others the interaction of ability, creativity and commitment (Renzulli, 1978).

•  Gagné's model distinguishes GIFTS (natural aptitudes) from TALENTS (developed achievement), with the environment and the child's own motivation as the catalysts between them (Gagné, 2004). This is useful because it makes the school's job — development — explicit.

•  In Ireland the Education Act 1998 (s.2), as enacted, included 'the educational needs of exceptionally able student

presentations.name: Twice exceptional (high ability plus SLD, ADHD or ASD)
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child who has both high ability and a learning difficulty or developmental condition — commonly dyslexia, ADHD, autism or DCD. Reis, Baum and Burke (2014) give an operational definition: high potential in one or more areas alongside one or more disabilities.

•  The core issue is MASKING in both directions: ability can compensate for the difficulty (so attainment looks age-appropriate and nothing is flagged), and the difficulty can hide the ability (so the child is seen only for what they cannot do).

•  The result is often a child whose output looks average, whose teachers see no problem, and whose parents see a child who is frustrated, exhausted or anxi

presentations.name: Understanding and responding to adult direction
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description, in referral-form wording, of how a child responds when an adult tells them what to do — whether they understand the direction, whether they act on it, how quickly, and what happens when they do not. It sits under general ability and comprehension in Part D because the first question is whether the child UNDERSTOOD.

•  Three quite different things produce the same observation of 'doesn't do what he's told': the child did not understand (language, general ability, hearing); the child understood but could not organise or start the action (attention, executive function); or the child understood and chose not to (motivation, relationship, anxiety, escape).
