presentations.name: Care-experienced children (foster, kinship, residential, aftercare)
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child or young person who is or has been in the care of the State — in general foster care, relative (kinship) foster care, residential care, or special care — or who is now in aftercare. In Ireland, Tusla is responsible under the Child Care Act 1991; the large majority of children in care are in foster care (check Tusla's current figures before quoting).

•  Care status is not a diagnosis and not a problem in itself. Care-experienced children as a group have lower average educational outcomes, but Sebba et al. presentations.name: Child protection and welfare concerns
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a situation in which there is reasonable concern that a child has been, is being, or is at risk of being harmed — through neglect, emotional abuse, physical abuse or sexual abuse — or where the child's welfare needs are not being met. Children First (2017) defines the four categories and gives examples.

•  Under the Children First Act 2015, psychologists are mandated persons. A mandated person who knows, believes or has reasonable grounds to suspect that a child has been harmed, is being harmed or is at risk of being harmed, above the threshold of harm set out in the Act, must report to Tusla as soon as practicable. presentations.name: Domestic violence exposure
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child living with, or who has lived with, domestic violence or abuse between adults in the home — physical, sexual, emotional, financial or coercive control. The Domestic Violence Act 2018 created an offence of coercive control in Ireland.

•  Children are not 'witnesses' only: they hear, see, intervene, are used by the abuser, and live with the aftermath. Callaghan et al. (2018) describe children as directly experiencing coercive control and developing their own coping strategies.

presentations.name: Parenting capacity concerns
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of concern about whether a parent or carer is able to meet a child's needs — for safety, care, emotional warmth, stimulation, guidance and stability — often in the context of parental mental illness, substance use, intellectual disability, domestic violence, or overwhelming stress.

•  Parenting capacity is formally assessed by Tusla social workers and, in court proceedings, by specialist assessors, usually using an ecological framework that looks at the child's developmental needs, parenting capacity and family and environmental factors together (Cleaver et al., 2011; Donald & Jureidini, 2004).

presentations.name: Family functioning difficulties
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of patterns in a family — communication, conflict, roles, boundaries, emotional responsiveness, problem-solving — that are affecting the child's wellbeing or school functioning. Examples: high parental conflict, separation or divorce, bereavement, sibling difficulties, a family member's illness or addiction.

•  Systemic approaches see the child's difficulties in the context of family relationships rather than located in the child alone (Carr, 2012). The McMaster model (Epstein et al., 1978) describes dimensions of family functioning — problem-solving, communication, roles, affective responsiveness, affective involvement and behaviour control — that can struct

presentations.name: Housing and economic problems
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child whose school life is affected by poverty, debt, food insecurity, overcrowding, poor housing, housing insecurity or homelessness — including families in emergency accommodation (hotels, B&Bs, family hubs).

•  DSM-5-TR lists housing and economic problems among 'Other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention' (Z codes — check specific codes); Part D (5.5) records it as 'DSM-5-TR Z-codes'. These are context, not disorders.

•  Effects on school are practical and emotional: long commutes from emergency accommodation, nowhere to do homework, poor sleep, hunger, missed school, shame, and disrupted friendships. Growing Up in Ireland data link e

presentations.name: Social exclusion, discrimination, acculturation difficulty
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child whose wellbeing or school functioning is affected by being excluded, discriminated against, or struggling to adapt between cultures — for example Traveller and Roma children, children of migrant families, children seeking or granted international protection, children arriving under temporary protection, LGBTQ+ young people, and children from minority faiths.

•  Berry (1997) described acculturation as the process of cultural and psychological change when groups meet, with strategies such as integration, assimilation, separation and marginalisation; acculturative stress arises when the demands of adapting outstrip resources.

presentations.name: Knowing which service does what, and the referral route
Multi-disciplinary meetings and your role in them
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A practitioner competence: preparing for, contributing to and following up on meetings involving several professionals and the family — for example Student Support Plan reviews, CDNT team meetings, Meitheal meetings, transition meetings, Tusla child protection conferences, and case conferences in special schools.

•  Part D lists it as 'Added' under 5.5. The EP's typical contribution is a psychological perspective on learning, behaviour and wellbeing; a formulation that links different views; and practical recommendations for school.

presentations.name: Professional and service boundaries
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Professional and service boundaries — what is not yours to do — your named development area'. A presentation about the ROLE, not the child: the case in front of you contains a question that belongs to another profession or service, and the risk is that you answer it anyway.

•  The EP's lane in Irish schools: assess learning, behaviour and wellbeing in context; formulate; consult with teachers and parents; recommend at the right Continuum of Support level; refer; support whole-school work (NEPS, 2007; DES, 2017). Diagnosis of medical and psychiatric conditions and medication advice sit outside it (PSI 2.2.2).

•  Boundaries run in two directions. OUTWARD: q

presentations.name: Classroom environment
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Classroom environment — Context, not a diagnosis', and at School Age: 'Classroom observation with the environment as the unit of analysis, not the child'. The physical and organisational features of the room that make learning easier or harder for everyone, and for this child in particular.

•  Covers: noise and acoustics; light and glare; temperature and air; visual clutter on walls; seating and sight-lines to the teacher and board; space to move; where resources are kept; routines and visual structure (timetables, signals); and group arrangement.

presentations.name: Teaching match
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Teaching match — Context, not a diagnosis'. The fit between the level, pace and method of what is being taught and where the child actually is — too hard, too easy, too fast, or in a form the child cannot access.

•  Gickling and Armstrong (1978) found that on-task behaviour, task completion and comprehension were best when material was at an 'instructional' level of difficulty and fell away when it was at 'frustration' level. Their instructional-level ratios are often quoted — check the source before quoting a figure.

•  Haring et al. (1978) described an instructional hierarchy — acquisition, fluency, generalisation, adaptation — so the question is also S

presentations.name: Curriculum demands
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Curriculum demands — Context, not a diagnosis'. What the programme itself asks of the child at this stage — the language load, the reading and writing volume, the abstraction, the pace of coverage, the assessment format — set against the child's profile.

•  In Ireland the frame is the Primary Curriculum Framework (NCCA, 2023) at primary, and the Framework for Junior Cycle (DES, 2015) at post-primary, which includes Level 1 and Level 2 Learning Programmes (L1LPs and L2LPs) for some pupils with general learning disabilities — check current NCCA eligibility guidance.

•  Demands shift at known points: the move from learning to read to reading to learn in midd

presentations.name: Attendance and transitions
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Attendance and transitions — Context, not a diagnosis'. The pattern of the child's presence in school (days absent, late arrivals, partial days, reduced timetables) and how they manage everyday transitions — arrival, between lessons, after break, after holidays or illness.

•  Attendance is described, not diagnosed: WHEN (days, times, after weekends or holidays), WHY (illness, family, avoidance, exclusion, reduced days), and what happens on the way in.

•  Kearney and Graczyk (2014) proposed a tiered (response-to-intervention) model for attendance: universal promotion for all, targeted support for emerging absence, intensive planning for chronic absence — w

presentations.name: Transition planning (early years to primary, primary to post-primary, school leaver)
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Transition planning (early years to primary, primary to post-primary, school leaver) — Not a diagnosis'. The planned movement of a child between settings, and the information, relationships and supports that need to travel with them.

•  Three main points in Irish practice: PRESCHOOL TO PRIMARY (NCCA Mo Scéal templates share information from the ECCE setting); PRIMARY TO POST-PRIMARY (the NCCA Education Passport, including the Sixth Class report and the child's 'My Profile'); SCHOOL LEAVER (further education, training, third level via DARE, employment, or HSE adult day services).

•  Evangelou et al. (2008) found successful primary–secondary transition link

presentations.name: Assistive technology
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Assistive technology — Not a diagnosis'. The whole question of AT as an access factor: what the child has, whether it matches the need, whether it is actually used, and whether it continues across classes, home, exams and transitions. (For the specific omission of AT never tried, see 'Assistive technology not yet trialled'.)

•  Ranges from low-tech (reading rulers, pencil grips, slant boards) through mainstream tools (built-in dictation, read-aloud, word prediction, keyboards) to specialist equipment (switch access, eye gaze, braille devices, FM/radio aids). AAC is covered separately in 'AAC and communication access'.

presentations.name: Reasonable Accommodations in State Examinations (RACE)
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Reasonable Accommodations in State Examinations (RACE) — Not a diagnosis'. The State Examinations Commission's scheme is formally 'Reasonable Accommodations at the Certificate Examinations' — arrangements at Junior and Leaving Certificate that remove barriers to showing what a candidate knows, without changing what is assessed.

•  WHO DOES WHAT: the school applies and, for learning-difficulty grounds, carries out the required testing; the SEC decides. The SEC's 2026 Instructions state that a psychological report is not required, a professional report's recommendation does not confer eligibility, and cognitive ability scores and diagnosis are not needed for

presentations.name: SNA and resource teaching allocation
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'SNA and resource teaching allocation — Not a diagnosis'. How additional adults are allocated to schools and then deployed around this child: Special Education Teaching (SET) time, and Special Needs Assistant (SNA) support.

•  SET ALLOCATION: since 2017 schools receive special education teaching allocations based on their educational profile, not on individual diagnoses or assessments, and deploy them by need using the Continuum of Support (Circulars 0013/2017 primary and 0014/2017 post-primary — check current versions; DES, 2017). An individual report is not needed to access SET support.

•  SNA ALLOCATION: the SNA scheme supports schools to meet the CARE

presentations.name: Home learning environment
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Home learning environment — Context, not a diagnosis'. The learning activities, routines, language and resources in the child's home — reading together, talk, play with letters and numbers, space and time for homework, access to books and devices.

•  The Effective Provision of Pre-School Education (EPPE) project found that what parents DO with children (reading, songs, letters, numbers, library visits) predicted early attainment more strongly than parental occupation or education (Sylva et al., 2004; Melhuish et al., 2008).

•  Desforges and Abouchaar (2003) concluded that 'at-home' parental involvement has a significant positive effect on attainment, acro

presentations.name: Community context
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Community context — Context, not a diagnosis'. The neighbourhood, community and wider systems around the child and school — economic disadvantage, rural isolation, housing, transport, cultural and ethnic community, local services and their waiting lists.

•  Bronfenbrenner's (1979) ecological model places the child within nested systems (microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem): community context sits in the outer systems but shapes what happens at home and in school.

•  In Ireland, DEIS (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools) targets additional supports — including Home School Community Liaison (HSCL) and the School Completion Programme —

presentations.name: Continuum of Support level and whether it was actually implemented
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Continuum of Support level and whether it was actually implemented — Added'. A SYSTEMIC question about the case: at what level of the NEPS Continuum of Support (Classroom Support, School Support, School Support Plus) is the child — and was the support at that level actually delivered, as planned, long enough to judge its effect?

•  The Continuum is a problem-solving model: identify the concern, gather information, plan, intervene, review; move up or down levels according to response (NEPS, 2007; NEPS, 2010; DES, 2017). The Student Support File is the record of that cycle.

presentations.name: Whole-school policy and practice
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Whole-school policy and practice — Added — your systemic change development area'. The school's policies, procedures and culture that shape how children are supported: SEN policy, code of behaviour, anti-bullying procedures, wellbeing, attendance, child protection, and how these are actually practised.

•  Irish frames: Wellbeing Policy Statement and Framework for Practice (DES, 2019 — check current version); code of behaviour guidelines (NEWB, 2008); Bí Cineálta anti-bullying procedures (Department of Education, 2024); Child Protection Procedures for Primary and Post-Primary Schools (check current version); School Self-Evaluation.

•  The EP's role: consul

presentations.name: Staff training need identified through casework
presentations.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Staff training need identified through casework — Added'. A systemic finding: individual cases reveal that staff lack knowledge, skills or confidence in a specific area (e.g., autism, anxiety, behaviour, literacy intervention), and that addressing this would help many children.

•  Joyce and Showers (2002) found that training with theory and demonstration alone produced little transfer to classroom practice; adding practice, feedback and in-class coaching greatly increased transfer.

•  Guskey (2002) argued that teacher beliefs often change AFTER they see improved outcomes from trying a new practice — so training should be linked to trial and feedback, not

skills.key: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic || Choose a method suited to the referral question
skills.why: Method choice is the single decision that determines whether an observation produces evidence or description. Momentary time sampling estimates how much of the time something occurs; partial interval over-estimates it; event recording counts discrete acts; narrative gives sequence but no prevalence.

skills.key: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic || Run a timed interval or event sample accurately
skills.why: An inconsistent interval makes every number meaningless, and an illegible grid means the data exists only in your memory — which is exactly what observation is supposed to replace. Hintze (2005) is clear that psychometric quality in direct observation rests on procedural consistency, not on the obse

skills.key: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic || Record antecedent, behaviour and consequence separately
skills.why: ABC recording is the foundation of a functional account — what happened before, what the child did, what followed. The discipline is keeping them separate, because the moment you write the cause into the description you have stopped observing and started concluding, and nobody reading the report can

skills.key: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic || Agree with the teacher how you will be introduced
skills.why: How you are introduced determines what you get to see. Introduced as 'someone here to watch Jack', you will observe a child who knows he is being watched and a class that knows it too. Introduced as 'someone here to see how the class works', you observe something much closer to ordinary. It is also

skills.key: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic || Position yourself to see without becoming the focus
skills.why: Where you sit changes what happens. Sitting at the child's table makes you part of the lesson; standing at the front makes you an inspector; sitting in the flow of the room means children route past you all morning. The aim is line of sight to what you came to see, out of the traffic, and low enough

skills.key: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic || Observe without altering what you came to see
skills.why: Reactivity is real and it is not eliminable — your presence changes the room. The competence is not in removing the effect but in minimising it, noticing it, and reporting it. An observation that does not mention reactivity is an observation whose author has not thought about it.

skills.key: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic || Note peer interaction and social positioning
skills.block: Block 3 · Knowing what to look at
skills.why: Where a child sits in the peer group is invisible in any test and is often the thing the referral is really about. It is also the domain where adult report is least reliable — teachers see the classroom, and most of what matters happens at break.

skills.key: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic || Note adult interaction and prompting patterns
skills.block: Block 3 · Knowing what to look at
skills.why: How much adult support a child receives is usually unrecorded and frequently the most important variable in the room. A child who appears to manage independent work may be receiving a prompt every ninety seconds. Nobody has counted, and the Student Support File will not say.

skills.key: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic || Observe the same child across two settings
skills.block: Block 3 · Knowing what to look at
skills.why: A single observation is a single day in a single room. Hintze (2005) found temporal stability in direct observation is modest, and cross-setting comparison is the cheapest correction available. It is also diagnostic in its own right — DSM-5-TR requires ADHD symptoms in two or more settings, and a ch

skills.key: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic || Keep description and interpretation separate
skills.why: This is the discipline that makes a report defensible. PSI 1.2.8 requires opinion to be clearly labelled as opinion and conjecture avoided. A report where the reader cannot tell what was seen from what was concluded is a report that cannot be checked — and it will be quoted back for years by people

skills.key: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic || Link what you observed to the referral question
skills.why: An observation that describes everything answers nothing. The referral asked something specific, and the observation exists to move that question forward — to support a hypothesis, weaken it, or show that the question was wrong. A thorough description that does not connect back is work nobody can us

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Prepare the history schedule and read it beforehand
skills.why: Reading a schedule for the first time in front of a parent costs you the two things the interview depends on: your attention, which is on the page instead of on them, and their confidence, because a psychologist reading questions aloud looks like a form-filler. Preparation is also what lets you depa

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Take pregnancy, birth and neonatal history
skills.why: Most of the time this rules things out, which is exactly why it is asked. Occasionally it explains a great deal — prematurity, hypoxia, neonatal intensive care, significant jaundice. The skill is asking without implying that you are looking for a cause in the parent, because that is how it lands if

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Take early motor, speech and language milestones
skills.why: Sequence is the output, not precision. Whether a child walked at 13 or 15 months rarely matters; whether language was delayed before behaviour became difficult matters enormously. Parental recall of milestone ages is moderately accurate at best and improves markedly with anchoring, so how you ask de

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Ask about sleep, feeding and self-care
skills.why: These three are skipped more than any others and they change the whole picture. A child sleeping six hours will present as inattentive, dysregulated and slow on every measure you administer. Feeding and self-care give you the adaptive functioning that a cognitive assessment cannot, and both are the

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Ask about play and peer relationships
skills.why: Play and friendship are where social communication shows itself, and parents see a side of it school never does — birthday parties, cousins, the estate, who calls for them. It is also the domain where a language-focused history misses the point entirely: a child can have adequate language and no rec

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Ask about medical history and medication
skills.why: Medication names alone tell you almost nothing. What matters is what it is for, what effect it has, whether it is taken consistently, and whether a dose changed recently — because a dose change three weeks ago can account for the entire referral. Hearing and vision belong here too, and a hearing his

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Open with the parent's own concern, in their words
skills.why: The parent's own framing is data you can get in the first two minutes and cannot get later, because once you have asked twenty structured questions they will answer in your terms. Their words also go in the report, and a report that quotes a parent accurately is one they trust.

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Ask about strengths before difficulties
skills.why: Asking about strengths first is not a courtesy. It changes what you get: a parent who has described what their child is good at answers the difficult questions differently, and you end up with a fuller account. It also gives you the material for the feedback session, where a strength you can evidenc

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Follow up an ambiguous answer rather than accepting it
skills.why: Ambiguous answers are where the information is. 'A few', 'sometimes', 'not really', 'he's grand' are all doors, and walking past them is the commonest way a history ends up thin. The difficulty is that noticing has to happen in real time, while you are also listening, writing and thinking about the

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Ask about family structure and significant events sensitively
skills.why: Family context sits at the environmental level of every framework you use, and significant events — bereavement, separation, migration, illness, a parent's own difficulty — frequently explain timing that nothing else does. PSI 1.2.1 restricts you to information germane to the purpose, so the skill i

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Manage emotional disclosure without losing the thread
skills.why: Parents cry in these interviews. It is ordinary and it is not a failure of the interview. The skill is responding as a person, without either brushing past it or abandoning the task — and knowing where your competence ends, because if the disclosure is about the parent's own mental health you are li

skills.key: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history || Close with what happens next and when
skills.why: An unclear ending is the commonest complaint parents make about psychology services. They leave not knowing what happens, wait, hear nothing, and conclude they have been forgotten. Two minutes at the end prevents it, and it is also where you set expectations you can actually meet.

skills.key: Structured interviewing of teachers and SET || Place the child on the Continuum of Support
skills.why: The Continuum is how Irish schools allocate. Recommending School Support Plus for a child already at that level, or Classroom Support for one who has exhausted it, tells the school you did not ask. Knowing the stage first also tells you what has already failed, which is the most useful thing in the

skills.key: Structured interviewing of teachers and SET || Ask what has already been tried and what happened
skills.why: Recommending something the school tried last year and abandoned is the fastest way to lose credibility. What was tried, how it was delivered, for how long, and what happened is also diagnostic: an intervention delivered at the wrong intensity that then 'did not work' tells you about delivery, not ab

skills.key: Structured interviewing of teachers and SET || Ask about presentation across the timetable
skills.why: A difficulty that appears in every lesson and one that appears only in English are different findings requiring different responses. Variation by subject points to task demand; variation by teacher points to relationship or approach; variation by time of day points to fatigue, medication or sleep.

skills.key: Structured interviewing of teachers and SET || Clarify the referral question with the person who raised it
skills.why: Referral forms are written quickly and often by someone other than the person who is worried. The question on the form and the question in the referrer's head are frequently different, and everything you do afterwards is aimed at whichever one you accepted.

skills.key: Structured interviewing of teachers and SET || Request standardised attainment data in advance
skills.why: Schools hold group test data you can have for the asking, and reading it beforehand changes what you assess. It can also answer the question on its own, which saves the child an assessment they did not need.

skills.key: Structured interviewing of teachers and SET || Ask who knows this child best in the school
skills.why: The person you are given is not always the person who knows. The SET who takes the child three times a week, the SNA who is with them at lunch, or last year's teacher may hold more than the class teacher. Asking takes one sentence and routinely changes the quality of what you get.

skills.key: Structured interviewing of teachers and SET || Agree what feedback the school gets and when
skills.why: Unset expectations produce two failures: a school that chases you, and a school that assumes it is getting something you never intended to give. Agreeing it at the start also forces you to decide what the school actually needs, which is usually less than the full report and sooner.

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Understand what each index measures
skills.why: You will be asked to explain an index to a parent within minutes of giving them a number, and a definition read off a manual does not survive that conversation. Understanding also governs whether you interpret correctly: Verbal Comprehension is acquired knowledge and reasoning with language, not voc

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Know what the test does not measure
skills.why: The limitations sentence is what separates a competent report from a technically correct one. WISC-V does not measure attainment, motivation, creativity, adaptive functioning, executive function in daily life, or anything about a child assessed in a second language without heavy caution. Saying so p

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Apply start points correctly for age and ability
skills.why: A wrong start point invalidates the subtest and, if you do not notice, the index it sits in. Start points vary by subtest and by age, and several allow an adjusted start for a child you suspect has lower ability — which is a judgement you have to make before you have any data on them.

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Apply reverse rules without hesitating
skills.why: Reverse rules exist so a child who fails at their age-appropriate start point gets credit for easier items they would have passed. Applied late or inconsistently, you underestimate the child. Applied with visible hesitation, you signal to the child that they have failed, which affects everything aft

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Apply discontinue rules correctly
skills.why: Discontinue rules protect the child from a run of failure and protect the score from being inflated by lucky guesses. The temptation is to continue past discontinue because stopping feels unkind — and it is the kindest thing available, because the alternative is a child sitting through items they ca

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Query and prompt only where the manual permits
skills.why: Over-querying inflates scores and makes the assessment uncomparable to the norms. It is also the single most common trainee error, because it comes from wanting the child to do well. The manual specifies exactly which responses may be queried and with what wording; anything beyond that is help, not

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Prepare and check the kit before the child arrives
skills.why: A missing block or a lost stopwatch mid-subtest costs you the subtest and the child's confidence in you. Kits get borrowed, pieces migrate, and the only reliable moment to discover it is before the child is in the room.

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Set up table and seating correctly
skills.why: The child must see the stimulus book clearly and you must see the record form without the child seeing it. Sitting opposite creates a test-like confrontation and makes the stimulus book hard to angle; sitting beside makes timing awkward. Corner seating usually solves both.

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Read instructions verbatim
skills.why: The norms were built on those exact words. Paraphrasing changes the task, and it happens most under time pressure or when you think the child has not understood — which is exactly when standardisation matters most. If a child genuinely cannot access the instruction, that is a finding, not a problem

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Time accurately while managing engagement
skills.why: Several subtests are timed and the timing is part of the score. The difficulty is doing it while also watching the child, recording responses and managing behaviour. Timing that slips because you were settling a child produces a score that is not comparable to anything.

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Record responses verbatim including errors
skills.why: Verbatim recording is what makes the protocol re-scoreable and what makes qualitative analysis possible afterwards. A child's wrong answer often tells you more than their right one — a Similarities response that is concrete rather than abstract is a finding you can only see if you wrote down what th

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Use the record form correctly including Q and P
skills.why: The record form is the legal and professional record of the administration. Q marks a query, P marks a prompt, and both must be visible to anyone re-scoring. An incomplete form means an unverifiable score, and it is the first thing an examiner looks at.

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Establish rapport before beginning
skills.why: Rapport is measurement validity, not manners. An anxious or wary child under-performs across every index, and you will then build a formulation on numbers that describe their state rather than their ability. Five minutes before subtest one is the cheapest investment in the whole assessment.

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Explain what will happen in language the child understands
skills.why: A child who does not know what is happening is managing uncertainty instead of doing the task. They also have a right to know — PSI 1.4 covers assent, and assent requires understanding. Telling them that some items will be too hard for everyone is the single most useful sentence available to you.

skills.key: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard || Notice fatigue, anxiety or disengagement
